claims.text: Controlled aging can induce a fine dispersion of coherent nanoprecipitates in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The nanoprecipitates will improve high-temperature strength through precipitation strengthening.
The aging treatment will preserve room-temperature ductility.
The aging treatment will not increase alloy density because it does not modify the overall composition.
The initial refractory alloy has a single-phase BCC or similar structure after high-temperature solution treatment.
A post-solution-treatment aging treatment can trigger in-situ precipitation of a minor coherent second phase.
The proposed benefit should apply during creep or tensile loading at approximately 1200 °C, including creep under 500 MPa for about 100 hours.
The precipitates formed during aging act as obstacles to dislocation motion at high temperature.
Dispersed precipitates hinder dislocation motion through mechanisms such as Orowan looping during high-temperature deformation.
Hindering dislocation motion will reduce creep rate and increase yield strength.
Small precipitate size and coherent interfaces will minimize adverse effects on room-temperature ductility.
Relative to the solution-treated baseline, the aged alloy will have lower high-temperature creep rate and higher yield strength.
Relative to the solution-treated baseline, aging will cause little or no loss of room-temperature performance.
The solution-treated, unaged baseline has satisfactory room-temperature properties but inferior high-temperature creep resistance.
The benefit requires an optimal precipitate size and volume-fraction range and precipitate stability up to approximately 1200 °C.
Over-aging or formation of incoherent brittle phases may impair both high-temperature and room-temperature performance.
TEM or SEM can be used to assess precipitate size, distribution, volume fraction, and the anticipated precipitate population.
